status.note: The simplest component in any library, chosen last on purpose: it is the first to exercise `axes` and `whenAxis`, which have sat in the schema since before this branch and have never been read by anything.

intent.purpose: Runs an action when chosen. It is the only component here that does something rather than holding something — nothing about a button's own state survives the click.
behaviour: Runs its action on click, and on Enter or Space when focused, because it is a button and the platform owns that.
Carries a rank — how much emphasis this action has relative to the others near it — separately from its colour. A secondary destructive action is both, and one axis could not say so.
Does nothing while disabled, and nothing while loading. Loading additionally announces that something is already in progress, so a second press is not silently swallowed.
Keeps its width while loading, so a row of buttons does not reflow when one of them starts working.
notFor: Navigation. A control that changes the URL is a link, and rendering it as a button loses the browser's own behaviour — open in a new tab, copy the address, see where it goes.
Holding a state. A control that stays pressed is a toggle button or a switch; this one forgets the moment it is released.
Choosing between options. That is a radio group or a select.
Carrying an icon with no label and no accessible name. An icon-only button needs a name supplied by the consumer, and nothing here can supply one.

hierarchy.description: How much emphasis this action carries relative to the others around it. The rank of the action, not its colour — a page should hold one primary action, and everything else ranks below it. Defaults to `secondary` rather than the canon's `primary`, because the common case is not the page's most important action and a default of `primary` makes every unconsidered button shout.

variant.description: What kind of action this is, which selects the colour role. Orthogonal to `hierarchy`: a secondary destructive action is `hierarchy: secondary` and `variant: danger`, and collapsing the two axes would make that unsayable. `success` and `warning` are in the canon and deliberately not taken — an action is not a status.

size.description: A contiguous subset of the canon's ladder. `xs` and `xl` are not designed for actions.

disabled.description: The platform's own disabled state. Removed from the focus order and cannot be activated.
disabled.visual: The whole control dims and the pointer cursor is dropped.

loading.description: The action is already running. The implementation must track this: no platform provides it.
loading.visual: A spinner replaces the leading icon and the label stays put, so the button does not change width.

hover.description: The pointer is over the button and it is neither disabled nor loading.

active.description: A pointer or key is held down — the CSS `:active` state.
active.visual: The surface shifts a second step, in the same direction.

focus-visible.description: Focused in a way the browser judges worth showing a ring for — keyboard, not a mouse click.
focus-visible.visual: A ring is drawn outside the button's box.

a11y.keyboard: Tab reaches it unless disabled. Enter and Space activate, which the platform provides.
notes: An icon-only button has no accessible name unless the consumer supplies one. Nothing here detects that, and it is the single most common accessibility defect in a design system's button.
`loading` must reach assistive technology as well as the eye. A button that visually shows a spinner and announces nothing tells a screen-reader user that their press did nothing.

`disabled` removes the button from the focus order entirely, so a keyboard user cannot land on it to discover why it is unavailable. Where the reason matters, the alternative is to leave it enabled and explain the failure on activation.

Contrast is claimed for the label against the button's own surface at every hierarchy and variant. It is NOT claimed for the button's surface against whatever a consumer places it on — a tertiary button on a coloured banner is the consumer's problem to check.

children.description: The label. Text, and a verb — a button named 'Settings' describes where you land, not what happens.

iconStart.description: An icon before the label. Decorative: the label carries the meaning.

iconEnd.description: An icon after the label, for an action that leads somewhere — a disclosure caret, an external-link mark.

root.description: The button. Owns the surface, the ring, the hit area and the rank.

iconStart.description: The leading icon, and the slot the spinner takes over while loading.

label.description: The text. Never wraps — a button that wraps to two lines is a link in disguise.
